h1: The 6 Best Portable Chargers Under $30 for Phones, Travel and Outages, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Portable Chargers Under $30: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 portable chargers under $30 scored on capacity, charging speed, built-in cables, size, wall plugs and magnetic hold.
summary: The Szfakuer 10000mAh slim power bank is the portable charger to buy for most people, with 22.5W USB-C charging, a 0.63 inch body and 8.11 oz weight. The citicr adds built-in cables and a fold-out wall plug, the VRURC four-cable model suits mixed devices, the IAPOS packs 40000mAh for outages and the Miady is a slim magnetic top-up.
intro: Capacity is the number everyone compares and the one that misleads most. A 10000mAh charger does not deliver 10000mAh to your phone, because the cells run at about 3.7V and the output runs at 5V or more, and conversion loses some on the way. The honest expectation is roughly two to three phone charges from a 10000mAh pack. Treat the maker's estimate of phone charges as the useful number, and discount it slightly.

So this ranking weighs charging speed, size and the cables you will actually carry, alongside capacity. We reviewed six portable chargers priced under $30 from their listings, comparing mAh, output wattage, port types, built-in cables and recharging method. The numbers on the box are maker claims, and real-world output depends on the cable and the phone.

products.name: Szfakuer 10000mAh Slim Power Bank
products.verdict: A 0.63 inch, 8.11 oz pack with 22.5W USB-C PD3.0 and QC4+ and three ports.
products.description:
The Szfakuer holds 10000mAh and charges at up to 22.5W over USB-C with PD3.0 and QC4+. It has two USB-A ports and one USB-C, and measures 0.63 inches thick at 8.11 oz.

It ranks first because 22.5W USB-C is the fastest output in this group short of the IAPOS, and a body under an inch thick fits a jacket pocket. PD3.0 and QC4+ cover most modern phones, and three ports let two devices charge at once. It has no built-in cable, unlike the citicr, so you must carry your own.

Buy it for everyday carry if you already own a good USB-C cable and want speed and size. Without a cable of your own, the citicr is more convenient.
pros: Three ports, two devices at once
products.idealFor: Everyday carry for owners who already have a good USB-C cable.
products.skipIf: You want cables or a wall plug built in.

products.name: citicr 10000mAh PD20W Power Bank
products.verdict: Built-in iOS and USB-C cables, PD20W fast charging and a fold-out AC wall plug.
products.description:
The citicr holds 10000mAh, offers PD20W and 22.5W fast charging, and has one iOS and one USB-C cable built in. It recharges through a fold-out AC wall plug.

It ranks second because it removes the two things people forget: a cable and a wall charger. The built-in iOS and USB-C leads cover iPhone and Android, and the fold-out plug means the bank recharges from any outlet without extra gear. It is slower than the Szfakuer on the USB-C port, and built-in cables are a common failure point, since a frayed lead cannot be replaced.

It suits a household with both iPhones and Android phones that wants nothing else in the bag. Treat the built-in leads as the weak link.
pros: iOS and USB-C cables built in
products.idealFor: Anyone who wants one device for iPhone and Android with wall recharging.
products.skipIf: You prefer to use your own cables.

products.name: VRURC 10000mAh Power Bank with 4 Built-In Cables
products.verdict: Four built-in cables including Micro USB and USB-C, five outputs and a lanyard.
products.description:
The VRURC holds 10000mAh with four built-in cables, including Micro USB and USB-C, and five charging outputs. A lanyard is included, and the USB-C port works in and out at 2.4A.

It ranks third because it covers devices that other banks ignore, such as older Micro USB earbuds, cameras and e-readers, alongside current phones. The USB-C port charges the bank as well as drawing power out. At 2.4A it is limited to basic speeds, nowhere near the Szfakuer's 22.5W, so a modern phone charges slowly.

Pick it for a family or traveler juggling older Micro USB gear and newer USB-C devices. Fast charging is not its strength.

keySpecs.value: 4 built in, incl. Micro USB and USB-C

products.idealFor: Families or travelers with older Micro USB gear and newer USB-C devices.
products.skipIf: You want fast charging for a modern phone.

products.name: VRURC 10000mAh Power Bank with AC Wall Plug
products.verdict: A 10000mAh pack with a built-in AC plug, Micro USB and USB-C cables and 2.5 to 4 phone charges.
products.description:
This VRURC holds 10000mAh and folds an AC wall plug into the body, alongside Micro USB and Type-C leads and spare data cables. The maker estimates 2.5 to 4 phone charges.

It ranks fourth because the wall plug makes it a charger and a power bank in one device: plug it into the wall to recharge it, then take it out for the day. The 2.5 to 4 charge estimate is realistic for a 10000mAh pack. It sits behind the citicr because it has no iOS lead and no stated fast-charge wattage, and it sits in the higher $25 to $50 bucket.

Choose it if you want the wall charger and the cable gone from your bag. Check the price, since it sits at the top of the $30 limit.

keySpecs.label: Cables
keySpecs.value: Micro USB and Type-C built in

products.idealFor: Travelers who want one piece of gear instead of a charger plus a cord.
products.skipIf: You use an iPhone with a Lightning port.

products.name: IAPOS 40000mAh 22.5W Power Bank
products.verdict: A 40000mAh pack with a 22.5W USB-A port, a 22W USB-C PD port and three devices at once.
products.description:
The IAPOS holds 40000mAh, with a 22.5W USB-A output, a 22W USB-C PD output and three simultaneous devices.

It ranks fifth because the size is its reason for being: 40000mAh is about four times a typical pack, enough for days of phone use in an outage or on a camping trip. The 22W USB-C PD output also charges a phone quickly. The tradeoff is weight and the airline rules, since a pack over 100Wh is restricted on flights, and 40000mAh at the usual 3.7V is about 148Wh. It is heavy to carry daily.

It is the pick for camping trips, long drives and storm season, when days of power matter more than weight. Do not plan to fly with it.
products.idealFor: Campers, drivers and outage planners who want days of power.
products.skipIf: You travel by air or want a pocket-size pack.

products.name: Miady 5000mAh Magnetic Power Bank
products.verdict: A 0.55 inch, credit-card-size magnetic pack with 5W wireless charging and five indicator lights.
products.description:
The Miady holds 5000mAh, snaps on magnetically and charges wirelessly at 5W. It is 0.55 inches thin and credit card size, with five indicator lights that show 25 percent each.

It ranks last because 5000mAh is half the capacity of the others and 5W wireless is slow, so it tops up rather than recharges. Its strength is convenience: it stays on the back of a phone with no cable. Wireless charging is also less efficient than wired, which cuts the usable charge further, and a case can weaken the magnetic hold.

Buy it for an iPhone owner who wants a slim, cable-free top-up that stays attached. For a full recharge, take a 10000mAh pack.
products.idealFor: iPhone owners who want a slim top-up that stays on the phone.
products.skipIf: You need a full recharge or fast charging.

whatMatters.detail: A 10000mAh pack is rated at the cell voltage of about 3.7V, and the output runs at 5V or more, so you get roughly two to three phone charges. Wireless charging loses more. Judge by the maker's charge estimate, and expect less than the printed number. Cable quality can cap charging below the port's rating, so pair a USB-C pack like the Szfakuer with a good cable.

A 22.5W USB-C PD output charges a modern phone far faster than a 2.4A port. A phone only charges as fast as its own limit and the cable allow. Look for PD3.0 or QC4+ on the listing, and use a cable rated for the speed. A phone's own limit sets the speed: a 22.5W output cannot push faster than the phone accepts.

Built-in cables save you from forgetting one, but a frayed lead cannot be replaced. They also fix the connector types you can use. Check which connectors are built in, and carry a spare cable if the pack depends on them. Built-in iOS or USB-C leads, as on the citicr and VRURC, save carrying one, but they cannot be swapped if one breaks.

A 10000mAh pack takes several hours to refill from a phone-style adapter. A fold-out wall plug lets you recharge from any outlet without a charger. Check how the bank recharges and whether the USB-C port works in both directions. Check that the pack charges while it powers a device, called pass-through, if you plan to run it from a wall plug overnight.

Most airlines allow power banks up to 100Wh in the cabin, which is about 27000mAh at 3.7V. Larger packs are restricted, and power banks must go in carry-on, not checked bags. Check the capacity before travelling with a 40000mAh pack. A 10000mAh pack stays well under that limit, while the IAPOS at 40000mAh does not, so read the rule before travelling.

faq.q: How many phone charges will I get from 10000mAh?
faq.a: Roughly two to three, which matches the VRURC's estimate of 2.5 to 4. The Szfakuer and citicr are rated at 10000mAh, but conversion losses mean you never get the full figure. Run times also depend on the phone's battery size.

Buying on capacity alone. A 40000mAh IAPOS is a big pack that you cannot take on a plane, and a 2.4A port on the VRURC charges a modern phone slowly. Check speed and size too. The 2.4A port is the limit to check on the VRURC.

faq.q: Is a portable charger worth it over a case battery?
faq.a: A separate bank like the Szfakuer works with any phone and doubles as a backup for other devices. A case battery is neater but ties you to one phone model and adds bulk. Case batteries cost more and cannot charge earbuds or tablets.

faq.q: How do I charge the bank itself?
faq.a: Use the USB-C input, or the fold-out wall plug on the citicr and VRURC AC model. A 10000mAh pack takes several hours, so plug it in overnight, and unplug it when it is full.

faq.q: How do I maintain a power bank?
faq.a: Keep it away from heat and water, and charge it every few months even when unused. Replace any bank that swells or gets very hot. Check built-in cables for fraying. Do not leave the pack in a hot car.

faq.q: Can I take it on a plane?
faq.a: Banks of 10000mAh like the Szfakuer are fine in carry-on. Packs above 100Wh, such as the 40000mAh IAPOS, are restricted by most airlines. Always carry power banks in the cabin, not checked bags. Keep the IAPOS out of checked luggage, and read your airline rules.

finalTake: The Szfakuer is the best portable charger for most people, because it combines 22.5W USB-C speed with a slim 0.63 inch body. The citicr is the better choice if you never want to carry a cable or a wall plug. The IAPOS is for outages and camping, and the Miady is a magnetic top-up only.
